chunks.text: If you need medicine, feel sick, or have a cold, this episode will help you.
I will teach you useful words, common phrases, and important questions that you may need at the pharmacy.
Visiting a pharmacy can be confusing if you don't speak the language well.
But don't worry, after listening to this episode, you will feel more confident when asking for medicine, understanding instructions, and talking to the pharmacist.
Part one, common words at the pharmacy.
First, let's learn some important words that you will hear at the pharmacy.
I will say each word slowly, and you can repeat after me.
Types of places and people.
Pharmacy.
A place where you buy medicine.
Pharmacist.
A person who gives medicine and advice.
Doctor.
A person who checks your health and gives prescriptions.
Customer.
A person who buys something at a store or pharmacy.
Types of medicine.
Medicine, a substance that helps when you are sick.
Prescription.
A document from a doctor for special medicine.
Pain killers.
Medicine that reduces pain, like aspirin or ibuprofen.
Antibiotics.
Medicine for infections.
Syrup.
Liquid medicine often used for coughs.
Pills, tablets, capsules, small forms of medicine that you swallow.
Cream ointment.
Medicine you put on your skin.
Symptoms and health conditions.
Cough.
When you make a sudden noise from your throat because of a cold.
Fever.
When your body temperature is too high.
Headache.
Pain in your head.
Stomachache.
Pain in your stomach.
Sore throat.
Pain in your throat.
Runny nose when liquid comes out of your nose.
Dizziness.
When you feel like everything is moving or spinning.
Other important words.
Dosage.
How much medicine you need to take.
Side effects.
Possible reactions to medicine like feeling sleepy or dizzy.
Allergic reaction.
When your body does not react well to something like a rash or swelling.
Expiration date.
The date when medicine is no longer safe to use.
These words will help you understand conversations at the pharmacy.
Next, let's learn useful phrases and sentences you can use.
Part two, useful phrases at the pharmacy.
Now, let's practice some useful phrases.
I will say each phrase twice.
Listen carefully and repeat after me.
Asking for medicine.
Do you have medicine for a cough?
I have a headache.
What do you recommend?
Can I buy this without a prescription?
Do I need a prescription for this?
Asking about dosage.
How often should I take this?
How many pills should I take per day?
Should I take this with food?
Can I drink alcohol while taking this medicine?
How long should I take this medicine?
Asking about side effects.
Are there any side effects?
Will this make me sleepy?
Can I drive after taking this?
What should I do if I feel sick after taking this?
Understanding instructions.
Take one pill every six hours.
Do not take more than two tablets per day.
Finish all the medicine even if you feel better.
Keep this medicine in a cool, dry place.
These phrases will help you communicate with a pharmacist and understand instructions for your medicine.
Now, let's go deeper into some important situations you may experience at the pharmacy.
Part three, common situations at the pharmacy.
Now, let's talk about different situations when you may need to visit a pharmacy.
I will describe the situation and give you some sentences that you can use.
One, buying medicine for a cold.
You have a cold.
Your nose is running and you are coughing.
You go to the pharmacy and ask for help.
Excuse me, I have a cold.
Do you have anything for a cough?
My throat hurts.
What medicine do you recommend?
Do you have a syrup for coughing?
Such two, asking about a prescription medicine.
Your doctor gave you a prescription and you need to buy the medicine.
Hello, I have a prescription from my doctor.
Can I get this medicine with this prescription?
How much does this cost?
Three, understanding how to use medicine.
You bought medicine, but you need to know how to use it.
How often should I take this?
Should I take this before or after meals?
Can I take this at night?
Four, asking about allergies or side effects.
You are worried about side effects or allergies.
I am allergic to penicillin.
Is this medicine safe for me?
Will this medicine make me sleepy?
What are the common side effects of this medicine?
By practicing these sentences, you will feel more comfortable speaking English at the pharmacy.
Now let's review everything we have learned.
Part 4 Summary and Practice
Great job!
Today we learned many important words and phrases for the pharmacy.
